images.filename: Arched gate from the A5 to the cemetery garden of St Cybi's church - geograph.org.uk - 742677.jpg
images.caption:
Arched gate in the east wall (toward the sea), from the lower courtyard cemetery of St Cybi's church onto Victoria Road (it's not the A5, which ends at the train station, south from here - see openstreetmap).  
This wall and arch are modern. They do not mark the eastern boundary of the Roman fort, because that part of the land was under water until the building of Holyhead's great breakwater. The lower courtyard was consecretad as cemetery in 1826. The eastern boundary of the Roman fort was on top of the small cliff that stands between the upper courtyard and the lower courtyard;  it shows here at the back of the lower courtyard, covered with greenery that is of a slightly darker shade than the grass. The tower that peaks up on the right of the gate's arch is the one that stand at the north-east corner of the fort's grounds.


The Welsh name for Holyhead is Caergybi which means Cybi's Fort.

images.filename: St Cybi's cemetery garden - geograph.org.uk - 742670.jpg
images.caption:
St Cybi's lower courtyard cemetery - which has not been "turned into a garden", it is still very much a cemetery albeit a nice & calm place. This lower courtyard was under water (during high tides) until the sea recessed subsequently to the building of Holyhead's great breakwater early 19th century). 
In the bottom right corner of the photo is the staircase that leads from the fort's and church's original courtyard, to what used to be the seashore until some 200 years ago (the lower courtyard). This staircase has an interesting design: it is rounded and has high walls, both to protect users from attacks, may it be from heavy sea waves or from assailants. 

The photo underlines how close the church is to Victoria Road (not the A5, which ends at the railway station further south)) and to the port facilities at Holyhead. Upper right, background: the metal curves of the Celtic Gateway footbridge.

images.filename: The site of the Roman Fort viewed from Victoria Road - geograph.org.uk - 744103.jpg
images.caption:
The site of the Roman fort viewed from Victoria Road. Note that the lower courtyard behind the wall was under water at every high tide, until early 19th century when the harbour underwent much transformation - in particular the building of the great breakwater, that made the shoreline recede down to where it is today. So the eastern boundary of the fort was at the top of the wall that we see covered with vegetation. The lower courtyard, claimed on the sea, was consecrated for use as a cemetery in 1926. The staircase that we see in that greenery also dates from early 19th century. 
 The site of this 4rd century fort has been occupied by a succession of Christian churches since the 6th century. It was built to withstand attacks by Irish raiders; the Roman Navy used the fort as a base from which to patrol the Irish Sea. There was a signal station on Holyhead Mountain (National Grid code : NGRef SH21880), installed by the Romans in a 7-hectare iron age hillfort called Caer-Y-Twr, from which reports of Irish vessels could be sent to the fort.

images.filename: The south facade of St Cybi's Church - geograph.org.uk - 742776.jpg
images.caption: The south facade of St Cybi's Church The features from the left are the tower, surrmounted by weather vane dated 1753, featuring a fish, the south porch and the twin windows of the south aisle. The south trancept occupies the centre of the photo, with the Stanley Chapel of 1879 on the right. Wm. Stanley, a major landowner, was a generous benefactor of both St Cybi Church and the town of Holyhead in general.

images.filename: The grave of a child of the Skerries - geograph.org.uk - 874253.jpg
images.caption: The grave of a child of the Skerries The Skerries are a group of rocks surrounded by treacherous waters 3kms north-west of Carmel Head and 12kms north this cemetery at St Cybi's Church. The Skerries light was the last private lighthouse in Britain and only came under the control of Trinity House in 1841. This little child of 4 would have been the daughter of the lighthouse keeper.

images.filename: Roman Wall around the site of St Cybi's Church - geograph.org.uk - 1414149.jpg
images.caption:
Roman wall around the upper courtyard of St Cybi's church, Holyhead, Holy Island, Anglesey, Wales. That corner is the north-west corner, with the north wall (and its modern portal) on the right and the west wall on the left. We can still see some remnants of the chemin de ronde or wall walk at the top of the walls. This was not and still is not the main entrance, which was and is on the south side (here ). 
According to Nash-Williams (1959) (see p. 99) and others, the fort was built around the years 350 to 380 to extend in the north-east the defense line against the Saxons, and to keep the Irish raiders out. It was abandoned around the middle of the following century, most probably when Caernarvon fort was evacuated - according to Pleiades, this was in 438. St Cybi's church was built in the compound around 540.

images.filename: St Cybi (8062261644).jpg
images.caption: St. Cybi is a truly ancient church. The original was built on the site of a monastic settlement dating back to 540 AD. It was founded within an abandoned Roman fort by St. Cybi, first cousin of St. David, the Patron Saint of Wales. The church of Saint Cybi in Holyhead has been sacked by Vikings in the 10th Century and then violated by the army of King Henry IV when he invaded Anglesey from Ireland in 1405, during the reign of Owain Glyndwr. Then during the English Civil War, Cromwell’s men were garrisoned at the church for several years, destroying the font, windows, statues and tombs.
